Empirical Research Plan: Land-Use Planning, Property Values, and Welfare in U.K. Cities
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
   • Primary: Staggered Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study specification.  
   • Why:  (i) Local planning authorities (LPAs) change their local plans, zoning maps, or introduce Article 4 directions at different calendar dates; (ii) the data track individual property transactions before and after those dates; (iii) we can compare price paths in LPAs that change regulations (“treated”) with those that do not (“controls”).  
   • Estimator: Sun & Abraham (2021) / Callaway & Sant’Anna (2021) group-time average treatment effects to avoid TWFE bias with staggered adoption.  
   • Secondary: 2-stage least squares robustness in which regulatory stringency is instrumented by plausibly exogenous central-government interventions (e.g., Housing Delivery Test penalties or court-imposed plan reviews).

2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  
   Treatment variable  
   • RegChange_it = 1 for property i in LPA l in year t ≥ τ_l, where τ_l is the first fiscal year in which the LPA’s local plan is formally adopted that either:  
        a) tightens height/plot-ratio limits or increases protected land share (stringency +) or  
        b) relaxes density limits or expands buildable land (stringency –).  
   • We code separate indicators: Tighten_l,t and Relax_l,t; baseline specification pools them with sign à la housing-supply model.

   Control group  
   • Properties located in LPAs that do not change their plan during the sample window, or that change only after the study horizon.  
   • For dynamic event-study graphs the counterfactual year k is the same LPA k-years before adoption (“not-yet-treated”) plus all never-treated LPAs.

   Timing  
   • Event date = fiscal year in which the plan is adopted and becomes material for planning applications (date of Secretary-of-State sign-off).  
   • We treat t = –1 (year before adoption) as the last pretreatment period.

3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  
   A1. Parallel Trends: Absent the regulatory change, treated and control LPAs would have experienced parallel trajectories in property prices and development activity.  
        – Plausible? Reasonable once we include rich controls (LPA-by-year macro covariates, regional time trends) and test visually with pre-period leads.  
   A2. No Anticipation: Market participants do not fully price-in reforms more than one year before statutory adoption.  
        – Plausible? Consult consultation dates; usually final plan content is uncertain until inspector’s report, so full capitalization in prices typically begins close to adoption. We will drop t = –2 and t = –3 if anticipation is detected.  
   A3. Stable Composition / SUTVA: Properties do not move between LPAs; treatment of one LPA does not directly affect prices in another (no cross-border spillovers).  
        – Plausible within commuting zones? Potentially violated; will include 10 km buffer dropping border properties in robustness exercise.  
   A4. Common Shocks: Macroeconomic shocks (e.g., Help-to-Buy) affect treated and control LPAs similarly after conditioning on region-year FE.  
   A5. Correct treatment timing: τ_l is accurately measured (use official adoption dates).  

4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATION  
   1. Policy endogeneity (LPAs choose to tighten when prices already rising).  
        → (i) Show flat pre-trends; (ii) control for LPA-specific linear trends; (iii) instrument with central-government-imposed plan reviews.  
   2. Spillovers across LPA borders.  
        → Exclude properties within 10 km of treated LPA borders; alternatively estimate spatial DID with border fixed effects.  
   3. Anticipation/announcement effects.  
        → Include leads up to four years; drop early leads if significant; alternatively redefine τ_l as date of plan publication (placebo).  

5. R CODE OUTLINE  
```r
# 0. Packages --------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)          # Sun & Abraham via sunab()
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)          # already loaded but kept for clarity

# 1. Load Data -------------------------------------------------------------
dt <- fread("uk_property_planning.csv")   # one row = property-year

# 2. Variable Construction -------------------------------------------------
# Convert dates
dt[, year := year(TransactionDate)]

# Create treatment dummies -----------------------------------------------
# lpa_adopt_year is pre-coded in the dataset
dt[, rel_year := year - lpa_adopt_year]              # event time
dt[, treat := as.integer(rel_year >= 0 & !is.na(rel_year))]   # treated observations
dt[, never_treated := as.integer(is.na(lpa_adopt_year))]

# Sun & Abraham interaction term
dt[, cohort := lpa_adopt_year]                       # adoption cohort
dt[, cohort := fifelse(is.na(cohort), 9999, cohort)] # 9999 = never-treated

# 3. Fixed Effects identifiers --------------------------------------------
# property id
dt[, pid := .GRP, by = .(PropertyID)]

# 4. Main Specification ----------------------------------------------------
est <- feols(
  log(Price) ~ sunab(cohort, year) +  
               PropertyChars + LocalEconControls,
  data = dt,
  cluster = ~LPA_ID,      # cluster at LPA level
  fixef = ~ pid + year    # property FE + year FE
)

etable(est, se = "cluster")

# 5. Plot event-study coefficients ----------------------------------------
iplot(est)

# 6. Robustness: Border-exclusion sample ----------------------------------
dt_border <- dt[DistanceToBorder > 10]  # km
est2 <- update(est, data = dt_border)
etable(est2, se = "cluster")
```
(Assume PropertyChars = bedrooms, age, tenure; LocalEconControls = unemployment rate, wage, population growth.)

6. EXPECTED RESULTS  
Economic theory (urban land-use and housing-supply models) predicts:  
   • Tightening regulations (density caps, green-belt expansion) reduce developable land supply → raise average property prices and slow construction.  
   • Relaxations (up-zoning) increase supply potential → dampen price appreciation.  
Magnitude priors (based on U.S. and U.K. literature):  
   • A one-standard-deviation increase in regulatory stringency may raise mean real house prices by 8–12 percent within five years.  
   • Conversely, major up-zoning could lower price trajectories by ~5 percent relative to trend.

7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (DID)  
C1: Parallel pre-trends visually/statistically verified …………… 1  
C2: No anticipation (insignificant leads) ……………………………… 0.5  
C3: No spillovers / SUTVA ……………………………………………… 0.5  
C4: Proper treatment/control classification ………………………… 1  
C5: Robust standard errors & inference (clustered at LPA) ……… 1  
Total (out of 5) = 4.0 → The design is credible but hinges on handling anticipation and spatial spillovers.
